summary: Describes how a JavaScript application controls the signaling of a multimedia session through the W3C RTCPeerConnection API and relates this to existing signaling protocols. It obsoletes RFC 8829.

subtitle: How a web page's JavaScript drives WebRTC call setup by creating, applying and exchanging session descriptions.

tldr.problem: WebRTC needs a way to set up, manage and tear down multimedia sessions, but different applications want different signaling protocols, such as SIP or something custom.
tldr.mechanism: JSEP leaves signaling to the JavaScript application. The browser's JSEP implementation creates offers and answers as SDP through calls like createOffer and createAnswer, the application applies them with setLocalDescription and setRemoteDescription, and ICE candidate handling is kept separate.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8829. The main change is that the bundle policy max-bundle is deprecated and replaced by an identically defined must-bundle.

today: RFC 9429 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2024. It obsoletes RFC 8829, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why JSEP Leaves Signaling to the Application
sections.content:
RFC 9429 describes how the W3C WebRTC RTCPeerConnection interface controls the setup, management and teardown of a multimedia session. WebRTC call setup focuses on the media plane and leaves the signaling plane to the application, because different applications may prefer SIP or something custom.

The key information to exchange is the session description. In the JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol (JSEP) the JavaScript application controls the signaling state machine through two interfaces: passing in local and remote session descriptions, and interacting with the ICE state machine. The JSEP implementation plus the application is called a JSEP endpoint.

The RFC also records alternatives it rejected: a built-in lightweight signaling protocol, direct APIs for each media component, and a getCapabilities API that would make the application build its own session descriptions.
sections.eli5: The browser knows how to make the call, but your web page decides how to send the invitation. That way each website can use its own way of sending messages.

sections.title: Signaling Model and Session Descriptions
sections.content:
JSEP does not specify a signaling model other than the need to exchange session descriptions as in RFC 3264 offer/answer. Addressing, retransmission, forking and glare handling are left entirely to the application.

Session descriptions use SDP syntax internally, wrapped in a SessionDescription object so that another encoding could be used later. Most applications can treat them as opaque blobs.

The initiator calls createOffer, then setLocalDescription, and sends the offer over its own channel. The remote side calls setRemoteDescription, then createAnswer and setLocalDescription, and returns the answer, which the initiator installs with setRemoteDescription. Applications use RtpTransceiver, RtpSender and RtpReceiver objects to control the media tied to each m= section, which are generally mapped 1:1.
sections.eli5: One side writes an offer note and the other writes an answer note. Each side files both notes, and the web page carries them back and forth.

sections.title: The Offer/Answer State Machine
sections.content:
Because the same description means different things locally and remotely, JSEP has both setLocalDescription and setRemoteDescription, and each description carries a type: offer, pranswer, answer or rollback.

While an offer is outstanding it is pending; after an exchange completes it becomes current. A provisional answer (pranswer) lets the answerer send early session parameters without freeing resources, while a final answer completes the exchange and releases unneeded resources such as extra ICE components, TURN candidates or video decoders. A rollback with empty contents returns the machine to stable and the previous descriptions.

For quick setup, the RFC prefers a final sendonly answer sent immediately, followed later by a new sendrecv offer once the user accepts, rather than a provisional answer, because a provisional answer leaves the exchange open and the caller cannot send an updated offer.
sections.eli5: It is a turn-taking game. You can only make an offer when it is quiet, and once someone answers, the game goes back to quiet. If you change your mind, you can undo your last move.

sections.title: Policies and Defaults
sections.content:
The PeerConnection constructor sets global parameters: STUN/TURN servers, the ICE candidate policy, the candidate pool size, the bundle policy and the RTCP multiplexing policy.

  • ICE candidate policy: all or relay. The default MUST be all. Relay-only hides location information at the cost of more TURN use.
  • Candidate pool size: the default MUST be zero, because pre-gathering uses STUN/TURN server resources for long periods.
  • Bundle policy: balanced (default, MUST), max-compat and must-bundle. The old max-bundle is deprecated and SHOULD be ignored.
  • RTCP multiplexing: require (default, MUST) or negotiate.

The bundle and RTCP-multiplexing policies MUST NOT be changed after the PeerConnection is constructed.
sections.eli5: When you start a call you pick a few settings, like how much to share about where you are. If you pick nothing, the safe, sensible defaults are used.

sections.title: ICE, Trickling and SDP Procedures
sections.content:
JSEP decouples ICE from the signaling state machine. Candidate gathering starts when a new or recycled m= section is added or when new ICE credentials signal a restart. Each new candidate arrives through an onicecandidate event, and a null candidate marks the end of gathering. With Trickle ICE the offer can be sent right away and candidates sent as they appear, so ICE checks start sooner.

Section 5 specifies how SDP is built and parsed. Session descriptions MUST use ICE (RFC 8445) and DTLS or DTLS-SRTP, and SDP security descriptions for SRTP keying MUST NOT be used. An initial offer starts with v=0, an o= line and an s= line, and the o= address SHOULD be non-meaningful such as IN IP4 0.0.0.0 to avoid leaking a local IP address. The initial m= port is the default 9 (Discard) and the proto is UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF.

Further sections cover video size limits through a=imageattr, simulcast through a=simulcast and a=rid, and how forking at the signaling layer maps onto provisional and final answers.
sections.eli5: Before the call, each side collects the different routes it could be reached by and shares them one at a time. Whichever works first gets used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Although JSEP is formally an API, the RFC says to treat it as an Internet protocol in which the application JavaScript is untrustworthy, so the threat model of RFC 3552 applies. JavaScript can call the API in any order with any inputs, including SDP that was not produced by createOffer or createAnswer, and the implementation MUST be prepared for bogus data.

Application authors should know that editing candidates out of SDP or suppressing trickled candidates does not stop the implementation from performing checks from them. Endpoints that want to conceal their public IP address MUST instead configure the ICE agent to use only relay candidates. The wider WebRTC security architecture is in separate documents, RFC 8827 and RFC 8826. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The browser cannot trust the web page to always do the right thing, so it double-checks. Hiding your address needs a special setting, not just deleting it from the note.
